summary: Sydney Frank Markham was a historian and archaeologist who studied at Wadham College from circa 1920 to 1923. He served as Secretary and later President of the Museums Association from circa 1928 to 1942.

Syed Ali Bilgrami worked in Indology and linguistics. He studied at Patna College, Lucknow, Roorkee, the Royal School of Mines, and London, later serving the Government of Hyderabad (1879–1901) and as Reader in Marathi at Cambridge (1901).

Syed Ameer Ali was a scholar of history, archaeology, and religious studies. He studied at Aliah University and the University of Calcutta (circa 1863–1869), later holding a post at the University of Calcutta from circa 1881 to 1884.

Syed Hasan Askari was a historian and Indologist who studied at Zila School Chapra, Langat Singh College, and Patna University. He succeeded Anant Sadashiv Altekar as Director of the K. P. Jayaswal Research Institute from 1968 to 1971.
Syed Nawab Ali worked in history and archaeology. In 1932, he is attested as Principal of Bahauddin College and Professor of Persian at Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda.
Sylvain Brocquet is a scholar of Indology and linguistics. He studied at the École Normale Supérieure from 1980 under Marie-Claude Porcher and later held a post at Aix-Marseille University.

Sylvain Lévi was an Indologist and scholar of Buddhist, Iranian, and Central Asian studies. Educated at the Sorbonne under Abel Bergaigne, he held posts at the EPHE, the University of Paris, and the Collège de France (1890–1935).

Sze-bong Tso specializes in Buddhist studies and sinology. He completed his PhD at the Australian National University between 1977 and 1982 under the supervision of Jan Willem de Jong and Tissa Rajapatirana.
Søren Sørensen was an Indologist. He held a post at Herlufsholm School from 1876 to 1878 and later served at the University of Copenhagen from circa 1887 to 1902.
Sāmaṇera Bodhesako worked in Buddhist studies. He founded Path Press and served as an editor for the Buddhist Publication Society.
Sīlaratano studied under Narada Maha Thera, Nyanaponika Thera, and Ajahn Maha Bua (circa 1977–2011).

Sōkō Morinaga was a scholar of Buddhist studies and philosophy who studied at Toyama High School and Daitoku-ji under Zuigan Goto and Sessō Oda. He was head of Hanazono University (1986–1994) and served at Daiju-in (1963–1995).

T. A. Gopinatha Rao was a scholar of Indology, history, and archaeology. He served as Tamil Assistant at the Archaeological Survey of India (circa 1899–1908) and Superintendent of Archæology in Travancore State (circa 1908–1919).

T. Chandrasekharan was an Indologist who studied under S. Kuppuswami Sastri. He succeeded T. R. Chintamani and is attested in 1951 as Professor of History of Sanskrit Language and Literature at Madras Sanskrit College.

T. Ganapati Sastri was an Indologist who earned a PhD from the University of Tübingen in 1924. From circa 1908 to 1926, he served as curator and editor across several Travancore and Trivandrum manuscript institutions.

T. Griffith Foulk works in Buddhist studies, sinology, and Japanology. He earned his PhD at the University of Michigan under Luis Oscar Gómez, taught there (circa 1987–1995), and later held faculty posts at Sarah Lawrence College.

T. K. V. Desikachar was a scholar of Indology, religious studies, and philosophy. He studied under Tirumalai Krishnamacharya from circa 1960 to 1989 and founded the Krishnamacharya Yoga Mandiram in 1976.

T. N. Ramachandran was an archaeologist and Indologist. He served as an archaeologist at the Government Museum, Chennai (circa 1928–1934), and later worked as curator of archaeology at the National Museum, New Delhi.

T. R. Chintamani was an Indologist who studied under S. Kuppuswami Sastri and earned a PhD from the University of Madras. He served at the Adyar Library and became Senior Lecturer in Sanskrit at the University of Madras in 1933.

T. R. V. Murti was an Indologist and philosopher who earned a D.Litt. from Banaras Hindu University under Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan. He held posts at Oxford, Banaras Hindu University (circa 1953–1967), and McMaster University (circa 1971–1974).
